title: Confucianism
description: Ren, li, the gentleman, and the debate over human nature

concepts.title: Confucius and the Analects
concepts.contentHtml:
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BCE) lived in the Spring and Autumn period, an era of declining Zhou royal authority and constant warfare among feudal states. His response was not metaphysical speculation but a programme of moral and political renewal grounded in self-cultivation.

The Analects (Lúnyǔ) is a collection of brief sayings and conversations compiled by his students. Two key terms anchor his ethics:

Rén (仁), often translated 'humaneness' or 'benevolence': the supreme virtue, expressing fully realised humanity in relation to others. 'Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself' — Confucius's negative formulation of the Golden Rule.
Lǐ (礼), 'ritual' or 'propriety': the inherited forms of conduct — manners, ceremonies, family rites — through which rén becomes concrete in social life.

concepts.title: The Junzi and the Rectification of Names
concepts.contentHtml:
Confucius's moral exemplar is the jūnzǐ (君子), the 'gentleman' or 'exemplary person' — originally a term for an aristocrat, which Confucius redefined as a moral rather than a hereditary status. The jūnzǐ is shaped by long study, ritual practice, friendship, and reflection.

Government, for Confucius, depends on the moral character of those who govern. 'If those above love ritual, the people will be easy to govern.' Coercion is a sign of failed leadership; example is the proper instrument of rule.

The rectification of names (zhèng míng): when names match realities — when a father is truly a father, a ruler truly a ruler — the social order coheres. When names slip, social bonds dissolve. This makes language and titles ethically loaded: to call someone 'parent' is to invoke responsibilities the term carries.

concepts.title: Mencius and Xunzi on Human Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
Two later Confucians divided over the question of human nature.

Mencius (Mèngzǐ, 4th c. BCE) argued that human nature is originally good. Everyone has the 'four sprouts' (sì duān): the heart of compassion (sprout of rén), of shame (righteousness), of deference (propriety), and of right and wrong (wisdom). His famous example: anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, before considering rewards or reputation. Moral cultivation is therefore the nourishment of innate sprouts, not their imposition from outside.

Xunzi (Xúnzǐ, 3rd c. BCE) reversed this. Human nature is bad: we are born with appetites that, left unchecked, produce conflict. Goodness is the artifice of culture — ritual, music, education — laboriously imposed on raw nature. The teacher and the sage are essential precisely because we are not naturally good.

Both agreed that the goal is moral perfection through self-cultivation; they disagreed about what one starts from. The debate has shaped East Asian thought ever since.

title: Daoism
description: The Dao, wu wei, and Zhuangzi's playful skepticism

concepts.title: The Daodejing
concepts.contentHtml:
The Dàodéjīng (道德经), traditionally attributed to Laozi (6th c. BCE, though the text likely reached its present form later), is one of the most translated books in human history. Its eighty-one short chapters resist systematic exposition.

The opening line sets the tone: 'Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào' — 'The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao.' The Dao (the Way) is the source and pattern of all things, but any name we give it captures something less than it.

The De (德) is the inner power or virtue by which a being is what it is — its way of expressing the Dao. The Daodejing recommends a politics and ethics of following the Dao: yielding to circumstance, valuing the soft and low, distrusting the active intervention that thinks it can reshape reality from outside.

concepts.title: Wu Wei and the Sage
concepts.contentHtml:
The signature concept is wú wéi (无为), often translated 'non-action' but better understood as effortless action or action without forcing. Wu wei is not passivity. It is acting with the grain of things, never at cross-purposes with the situation.

The Daoist sage governs by wu wei: 'The sage does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.' Heavy-handed legal codes and constant interference produce the disorder they aim to prevent. The fewer prohibitions, the fewer thieves; the less ostentatious wealth, the less envy.

The Daodejing's political vision is anti-statist in flavour, valuing small communities, simple living, and rulers who are barely noticed. 'The best rulers, the people scarcely know exist.'

concepts.title: Zhuangzi: Skepticism, Equality, Transformation
concepts.contentHtml:
The Zhuangzi (4th c. BCE), a far stranger and more playful work, treats the same intuitions through stories, paradoxes, and dialogues with talking trees and butterflies.

The butterfly dream: 'Once Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly. Suddenly he awoke and was solidly Zhuang Zhou. He did not know whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was a man.' The story uses dreaming to undo the easy certainty of any single perspective.

The cook cutting up an ox: a master butcher's blade slips through joints because he 'follows the natural makeup' rather than chopping. After nineteen years his blade is as sharp as new. Skill, for Zhuangzi, is alignment with the patterns inherent in things.

His radical equalising of perspectives — 'this' and 'that' depend on the standpoint of judgement — anticipates much later perspectivism. But Zhuangzi is not a philosopher of bewilderment; the equalising is a way of releasing oneself from the rigid distinctions that make life painful, freeing one to wander 'beyond the dust and grime of the world'.

concepts.title: The Upanishads
concepts.contentHtml:
The Upaniṣads (composed ca. 800–200 BCE) are dense, often poetic philosophical dialogues that conclude the Vedic corpus — the name vedānta means 'end of the Vedas'.

Their central preoccupation is the relation between two terms. Ātman is the innermost self — not the empirical ego but the consciousness-witness behind all experience. Brahman is the ultimate reality, the absolute that underlies the world.

The Upaniṣadic great sayings (mahāvākyas) declare the identity of the two. Tat tvam asi: 'That thou art.' Aham brahmāsmi: 'I am Brahman.' Liberation (mokṣa) is recognition of this identity — release from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) by seeing through the false sense of a separate self.

concepts.title: Advaita Vedānta and Śaṅkara
concepts.contentHtml:
Several schools of Vedānta developed by interpreting the Upaniṣads. The most influential is Advaita ('non-dual') Vedānta, systematised by Śaṅkara (8th c. CE).

For Śaṅkara only Brahman is truly real. The world of multiplicity is māyā — not exactly illusion in the sense of unreal, but an appearance superimposed on Brahman through ignorance (avidyā). The standard analogy: a rope mistaken for a snake in dim light. The snake is not nothing — it produces fear — but it is not what is really there.

Realisation that ātman is brahman is not the achievement of a new state but the removal of a misperception. The point is not to become liberated but to recognise that one is, and always has been, brahman. Other Vedānta schools — Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita (qualified non-dualism) and Madhva's Dvaita (dualism) — disputed this radical non-duality, defending a real personal relation between devotee and God.

concepts.title: Sāṃkhya Dualism
concepts.contentHtml:
Sāṃkhya, one of the oldest of the six orthodox darśanas, offers a different ontology. Reality has two ultimate principles:

Puruṣa: pure consciousness, the witness — many, eternal, inactive.
Prakṛti: primal nature, the substrate of the changing world — one, dynamic, unconscious.

Prakṛti unfolds through three guṇas (qualities): sattva (clarity, lightness), rajas (activity, passion), tamas (inertia, dullness). Their changing proportions generate the manifold of mind and matter.

The bondage that produces suffering is the false identification of puruṣa with prakṛti — taking oneself to be the body, the emotions, the ever-changing thoughts. Liberation is discrimination (viveka): the puruṣa recognises itself as pure witness, and prakṛti's display becomes mere spectacle. The Yoga school adopts Sāṃkhya's metaphysics and adds practical disciplines for achieving this discriminative knowledge.

title: Buddhist Philosophy
description: Four Noble Truths, no-self, and Nāgārjuna's emptiness

concepts.title: The Four Noble Truths
concepts.contentHtml:
The Buddha (Siddhārtha Gautama, traditionally 5th–4th c. BCE) framed his teaching around four interlocking truths:

1. Duḥkha: existence as we ordinarily experience it is unsatisfactory — not only painful but pervaded by impermanence and unease, even at its most pleasurable.
2. Samudaya: the cause is craving (tṛṣṇā) and the ignorance (avidyā) that grasps things as more permanent and more separate than they are.
3. Nirodha: the cessation of craving brings release (nirvāṇa).
4. Magga: the path is the Eightfold Path — right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

The teaching is diagnostic and therapeutic: a doctor identifies the illness (truth 1), the cause (truth 2), the prognosis (truth 3), and the prescription (truth 4). Metaphysical speculation that does not contribute to liberation is famously treated by the Buddha as the wrong question — the parable of the man shot with a poisoned arrow who refuses treatment until he knows the archer's caste.

concepts.title: Anātman and Dependent Origination
concepts.contentHtml:
Two doctrines distinguish Buddhist analysis sharply from Vedānta.

Anātman (no-self): there is no permanent, unitary self underlying experience. What we call 'I' is a constantly changing aggregate of five skandhas (heaps): form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness. The intuition of a soul is precisely the misperception that produces craving.

Pratītya-samutpāda (dependent origination): everything that arises does so in dependence on conditions. There is no thing with intrinsic existence (svabhāva) — every entity is what it is only through its relations. The classical formula links twelve links from ignorance through name-and-form, sensation, craving, and grasping to birth, aging, and death.

The two doctrines are connected: because nothing has intrinsic existence, the self too must be conceived as a process, not a substance. Liberation is not the soul's escape but the dissolution of the very illusion of a separate, persisting self.

concepts.title: Nāgārjuna and Emptiness
concepts.contentHtml:
Nāgārjuna (ca. 2nd–3rd c. CE) founded the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. His Mūlamadhyamakakārikā uses rigorous dialectic to argue that all things are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature.

Nāgārjuna's strategy is to take any substantial concept (motion, causation, time, the self) and show it dissolves under analysis when treated as having intrinsic existence. The famous tetralemma: for any thesis P, we can deny that things are P, that they are not-P, that they are both, that they are neither.

Emptiness is not nihilism. Nāgārjuna distinguishes two truths: conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the everyday level on which things function and we make distinctions; and ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the level on which all things are empty of intrinsic nature. Emptiness applies even to emptiness itself — there is no privileged Absolute hidden behind the conventional. This is Nāgārjuna's 'middle way' between substantialism and annihilationism.

title: Zen and East Asian Buddhism
description: Chán, sudden enlightenment, Dōgen, and the kōan

concepts.title: From Madhyamaka to Chán
concepts.contentHtml:
Buddhism reached China by the 1st c. CE and was transformed by encounter with Daoist and Confucian thought. Out of this fusion, by the 6th–7th c., emerged Chán (禅, from Sanskrit dhyāna, 'meditative absorption'), known in Japan as Zen.

Chán inherits Madhyamaka's emptiness but reformulates it in distinctively East Asian terms. Influence from Daoism shows in the suspicion of words and the rhetoric of naturalness; influence from Yogācāra Buddhism (the 'consciousness-only' school of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu) shows in the focus on the mind that perceives.

The legend traces Chán to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk arriving in China around 520 CE, who is supposed to have meditated facing a wall for nine years. The historicity is doubtful; the legendary template — direct transmission outside scripture, pointing to the mind, seeing one's nature and becoming Buddha — has shaped the tradition's self-understanding ever since.

concepts.title: Sudden vs. Gradual Enlightenment
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 8th c. Chán split over how awakening (satori) occurs.

The Northern school, associated with Shenxiu, taught a gradual path: the mind is like a mirror, polished free of dust through long practice.

The Southern school, associated with Huineng (the sixth patriarch), taught sudden enlightenment: the mind is already buddha-nature; there is no mirror to polish. Enlightenment is the immediate recognition of what was always already the case, not an accumulation of merit.

The Southern view eventually prevailed, but with a crucial qualification: 'sudden' awakening still required disciplined practice. The slogan of the Linji (Rinzai) lineage — see your nature and become Buddha — assumed years of training. The split between sudden and gradual continues to structure Zen pedagogy: how can practice prepare for an event that cannot be earned by effort?

concepts.title: Dōgen and the Kōan
concepts.contentHtml:
Dōgen Kigen (1200–1253), founder of the Sōtō Zen lineage in Japan, gave Zen one of its most rigorous philosophical articulations. His Shōbōgenzō ("Treasury of the True Dharma Eye") is a body of essays of remarkable depth.

Dōgen's signature concept is shushō ittō, the unity of practice and realisation. To sit in zazen is not a means to enlightenment; the seated meditation is enlightenment. This dissolves the gap between path and goal that gradualism presupposes.

Equally striking is his treatment of being-time (uji): time is not a container in which beings reside; each being is a particular time. To be is to time, and to time is to be.

The Rinzai lineage made the kōan central — a brief story or exchange ('What is the sound of one hand clapping?', 'Does a dog have buddha-nature? Mu!') given to a student to break the grip of conceptual thought. The kōan is not a riddle to be solved but a device for exhausting the discursive mind, allowing the immediate recognition that Zen calls kenshō (seeing one's nature).
